title: Zhou dynasty and the Warring States
summary: The Zhou dynasty (1046–256 BCE) was the longest lasting in China's history. It justified overthrowing the Shang through the Mandate of Heaven. After nobles moved the capital east to Luoyang, royal authority steadily broke down, and in the Warring States period (475–221 BCE) smaller states consolidated into seven strong rivals. New ideas flourished in these centuries, including Confucianism and Daoism, before Qin unified China.

uncertainty.note: World History Encyclopedia dates the Zhou royal dynasty 1046–256 BCE (ending when Qin deposed the last Zhou king); the Smithsonian dates the dynasty and the culminating Warring States period to ca. 1050–221 BCE, ending with Qin's final unification.

reviewer_note: The record runs to 221 BCE to include the Warring States, although the Zhou dynasty itself ended in 256 BCE. Sources differ on whether the Mandate of Heaven was a new Zhou idea or developed from Shang concepts. The pin is Luoyang, the Eastern Zhou capital.
